::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 9) you can:

1. **execute** WL color refinement to stability by hand and state exactly what matching and differing histograms each prove;
2. **state and sketch** the proof that message-passing GNNs are bounded by 1-WL, and that GIN's injective sum reaches that bound (and why mean/max fall short of it);
3. **exhibit** graph pairs message passing cannot distinguish and explain the failure via identical computation trees;
4. **define** oversmoothing and oversquashing as distinct pathologies, diagnose which one a failing model has, and match each to its mitigations;
5. **choose** a rung on the expressiveness ladder — structural features, positional encodings, higher-order GNNs — knowing what each buys and what each costs.
:::

## The challenge was rigged

Two weeks ago, [the multiset widget](07-gnn-design.qmd) issued a standing
challenge: build two *different* neighborhoods that fool mean, max, **and** sum at
once. If you spent time on it, you noticed something suspicious. Within the
widget's rules — every feature a teal or gold one-hot — you can fool mean and max
together easily ($\{t\}$ vs $\{t,t\}$ does it), but sum always survives. Add a
node and the sum's first coordinate ticks up; swap a color and the coordinates
trade a unit. Nothing you build escapes it.

That was not bad luck. It was a theorem, planted where you could trip over it.
With one-hot features, the sum *is* the multiset: its $i$-th coordinate literally
counts how many neighbors carry color $i$, so two different multisets produce two
different sums, always. The challenge was impossible by construction — and the
impossibility is the engine of this entire lecture, because "sum preserves the
multiset" is precisely the property that will carry message passing all the way up
to a fifty-year-old algorithm from Soviet mathematics, and no further.

Outside the widget's rules, the challenge falls immediately. Allow raw real-valued
features and take $\{0, 2, 2, 2\}$ against $\{1, 1, 2, 2\}$: same size, same sum
(6), same mean (1.5), same max (2) — three aggregators, all fooled by two honestly
different neighborhoods. You proved the general version of this in
[HW2](../homeworks/hw2.qmd) with $\{1,3\}$ vs $\{2,2\}$: sum's injectivity is a
statement about *countable, embedded* features, not about raw numbers, which is
why GIN carries an MLP to embed first and sum second. Keep both halves of the
story: sum-over-embeddings loses nothing; everything else loses something.

So the local question — which aggregators can tell two *neighborhoods* apart — is
settled, and the answer is "sum, exactly." Today's question is global and much
sharper. Suppose you take the best possible aggregator, the best possible update,
unlimited width, unlimited depth, perfect training. **Which graphs can message
passing, as a class, never tell apart?** The answer has a name, a birth year
(1968), and a shape you can hold in your hand by the end of the hour.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Week 6 ended with two graphs — two triangles versus
one hexagon — that a GCN with uniform features provably cannot distinguish, and
the [sample exam](../exams/midterm-sample.qmd) made you prove it. Guess: is that
failure specific to the GCN's averaging, or does *every* architecture from Week 7
— GraphSAGE, GAT, GATv2, GIN — fail on the same pair?

::: {.predict-answer}
Every single one, GIN included, and by the end of §3 you will be able to prove it
in two sentences: all ten nodes across both graphs have identical unrolled
computation trees, and every message-passing network — whatever its aggregator,
attention, or update — computes its embedding as a function of that tree. Same
tree, same embedding, same pooled readout. The fix is not a better aggregator;
it is changing what the nodes *know* before the first message is sent (§6).
:::
:::

## The 1968 algorithm, formalized at last

You met <span class="term" data-def="Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement: repeatedly recolor every node by the pair (own color, multiset of neighbor colors) until the partition stops changing.">WL color refinement</span>
in [Week 2](02-classical-graph-ml.qmd) as a fast graph fingerprint, and you ran it
on the midterm. This week it stops being a trick and becomes the *measuring stick
of the field*, so let us state it with the care a measuring stick deserves.

Every node starts with the same color (or its feature value, if features exist).
One round of refinement recolors every node $v$ by the pair

$$c^{(t+1)}(v) = \mathrm{HASH}\!\left(c^{(t)}(v),\ \{\!\!\{\, c^{(t)}(u) : u \in N(v) \,\}\!\!\}\right)$$ {#eq-w09-wl}

where — $c^{(t)}(v)$ is node $v$'s color after round $t$ (round 0 is the shared
initial color); $N(v)$ is $v$'s set of neighbors, the same object Weeks 6–7
wrote calligraphically as $\mathcal{N}(v)$ — this week we use the theory
literature's plain $N(v)$; $\{\!\!\{\cdot\}\!\!\}$ is a multiset — order-free,
multiplicity-aware; and HASH assigns each distinct pair a fresh color,
consistently across *both* graphs being compared. Rounds repeat until the
partition of nodes into color classes stops refining, which takes at most $n$
rounds (each round either splits some class or changes nothing, and there are
only $n$ nodes to split).

You already own the single-graph procedure: Week 2's color-refinement float
stated it exactly as [Weisfeiler and Leman, 1968](https://www.iti.zcu.cz/wl2018/pdf/wl_paper_translation.pdf)
conceived it, one graph plus a shared signature table. This week's use is the
*two-graph comparison* that the shared table was built for, and it deserves its
own listing because the sharing is the entire point:

::: {#alg-w09-wl-compare .algorithm name="WL Comparison with a Shared Color Table"}
Decides whether refinement can certify two graphs as different, by comparing
their color histograms round by round.

**Input:** graphs $G_1, G_2$; rounds $T$ (with $n$ the larger node count,
$T \le n$ suffices). **Output:** "non-isomorphic (certified)" or "WL abstains".

1. $c(v) \leftarrow 0$ for every node of *both* graphs (or the node's feature value)
2. **for** round $t = 1 \ldots T$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each node $v$ of either graph: $\mathit{sig}(v) \leftarrow \bigl(c(v),\ \{\!\!\{\, c(u) : u \in N(v) \,\}\!\!\}\bigr)$
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;build ONE table over *both* graphs' signatures: new $\mathit{sig} \mapsto$ fresh color
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$c(v) \leftarrow \text{table}[\mathit{sig}(v)]$ for every node of both graphs
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$h_1, h_2 \leftarrow$ color counts of $G_1$, $G_2$
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**if** $h_1 \neq h_2$ **then** **return** "non-isomorphic (certified)"
8. **end for**
9. **return** "WL abstains"
:::

Everything Week 2's float did per graph happens in lines 3–5; what is new is
that line 4's table spans both graphs — same signature, same color, everywhere
— so the histograms of line 6 are *comparable*: six nodes of color 3 versus six
nodes of color 4 is a difference, not a match, and a per-graph table would
silently erase it. Each round costs one pass over both edge sets, $O(m)$ with
sorted buckets. Lab 9's exercise 1 has you implement exactly this
(`wl_histograms`), and its assertion ladder names the shared-table mistake for
you if you make it. Note also the asymmetry of line 7 versus line 9 — a verdict
versus a shrug — which is worth a formal name:

::: {#def-w09-wl-dist .definition name="WL-distinguishable"}
Two graphs are **WL-distinguishable** if at some round their color *histograms*
(computed under a shared table, @alg-w09-wl-compare) differ; if the histograms
stay identical all the way to stability, WL **abstains**. Reading guidance: the
definition is deliberately one-sided — distinguishable is a proved fact,
abstention is the absence of one, and @prp-sound below is the license for that
reading.
:::

Run it yourself — the widget executes @alg-w09-wl-compare, one click per round,
with a color table shared across both graphs so your eyes can do the comparing:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w9-wl.html >}}

The three presets are the week in miniature. The first pair — two triangles
versus one hexagon — never splits: every node has degree 2, every node forever
sees "two neighbors of my color," and the histograms stay locked at $\{6\}$ while
the graphs sit there being obviously different. The third pair is the antidote to
despair: $P_4 \cup P_3$ and $P_5 \cup P_2$ have the *same degree sequence* (four
degree-1 nodes, three degree-2 nodes each), so round 1 cannot separate them — but
round 2 can, and this pair deserves a full hand-trace because it is exactly the
kind of question the final exam likes.

Name the paths: $a\!-\!b\!-\!c\!-\!d$ and $e\!-\!f\!-\!g$ on the left;
$p\!-\!q\!-\!r\!-\!s\!-\!t$ and $u\!-\!v$ on the right. Round 1 colors by
degree: on both sides, four nodes get the leaf color 1 and three get the
interior color 2 — histograms $\{4, 3\}$ and $\{4, 3\}$, no split, exactly as
the degree-sequence argument predicted. Round 2 is where context enters — trace
every node's signature (own color, neighbor-color multiset) and watch three
exclusives appear:

| node | side | round-1 color | sees | signature exclusive to… |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $a, d, e, g$ | left | 1 (leaf) | $\{2\}$ | — (both sides: $p, t$ match) |
| $b, c$ | left | 2 (interior) | $\{1, 2\}$ | — (both sides: $q, s$ match) |
| $f$ — middle of $P_3$ | left | 2 (interior) | $\{1, 1\}$ — *two leaves* | **left** |
| $r$ — center of $P_5$ | right | 2 (interior) | $\{2, 2\}$ | **right** |
| $u, v$ — all of $P_2$ | right | 1 (leaf) | $\{1\}$ — a leaf seeing a leaf | **right** |

Three fresh colors appear on exactly one side each, the histograms diverge, and
refinement has proved in two rounds what degrees alone never could. The split
is not a lucky single collision; by round 2 the two graphs disagree in three
color classes simultaneously. WL sees strictly further than degree, than degree
sequences, and — as it keeps refining — than most anything cheap.

And the second preset is the one to remember when someone tells you these
failures are contrived toys:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w9-molecules.html >}}

Decalin and bicyclopentyl are real chemicals — a fused pair of hexagons and a
bonded pair of pentagons, both $C_{10}$ skeletons, both with exactly two
degree-3 carbons and eight degree-2 carbons. Run refinement (the widget will do
it in three clicks): both graphs stabilize at three color classes with counts
2, 4, 4 — the two ring-junction carbons, the four carbons adjacent to a junction,
the four carbons one step further out. Identical histograms, permanently.
1-WL — and therefore, by §3, every message-passing GNN reading these skeletons
with atom-type features alone — is structurally incapable of telling two distinct
molecules apart. Molecular property prediction is one of the largest industrial
applications of GNNs. The ceiling is not a curiosity; it ships in production.

Let us also be precise about the *direction* of the guarantee, because it is the
part everyone garbles under exam pressure and the part the midterm tested:

::: {#prp-sound .proposition name="WL is sound, not complete"}
If WL's histograms differ at any
round, the graphs are not isomorphic. If the histograms agree at every round, the
graphs may or may not be isomorphic — WL proves nothing.
:::

<details>
<summary>Proof (two sentences, worth owning)</summary>
An isomorphism maps nodes to nodes preserving adjacency, so by induction on
rounds it maps color classes to color classes bijectively — isomorphic graphs
produce identical histograms at every round, and differing histograms therefore
certify non-isomorphism. For the converse there is nothing to prove: two
triangles versus one hexagon agree at every round and are not isomorphic.
$\square$
</details>

The asymmetry has a practical reading you should carry into every use of WL and
of GNNs alike: a *split* is information, a *non-split* is silence. WL can convict
(these graphs differ) but never acquit (these graphs are the same) — and since
message passing lives below WL, a GNN giving two inputs the same representation
is silence too, never evidence of sameness.

One more calibration before the theory: how blind is WL *in practice*? Far less
than this lecture's parade of counterexamples suggests, and saying so is part of
honest teaching. On random graphs, one round of refinement already
individualizes almost every node — the counterexamples all live in highly
symmetric families (regular graphs, and *circulants* — rings with skip edges,
like §5's CSL family — chief among them) that
nature produces rarely and adversaries produce constantly. That skew explains a
fact of history you already touched in [Lab 2](../labs/lab02.qmd): before GNNs,
the *Weisfeiler–Leman subtree kernel*
([Shervashidze et al., 2011](https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a.html))
— run refinement for $h$ rounds, count
each color, and use the concatenated color histograms as a feature vector fed
to an SVM — was the reigning champion of graph classification, and your own
PROTEINS classifier at 70.4% was a member of that dynasty.

The kernel view is
worth thirty seconds of contemplation, because it makes this week's theorem
almost obvious in hindsight: the WL kernel's feature map assigns each graph the
census of its nodes' computation-tree shapes, a GNN's pooled readout is a
learned, compressed function of the same census, and the fifty-year detour from
1968 to 2019 was the field noticing that the two pipelines share an input.

When
the deep-learning wave arrived, the kernels did not lose because they saw less
— they see *exactly* as much, that is the theorem — but because histograms
cannot interpolate: two graphs with disjoint color sets share no features even
when their trees are one leaf apart, while a GNN's continuous embeddings degrade
gracefully. Discreteness, not blindness, was the kernels' ceiling; blindness
they bequeathed to their successors intact.

<details>
<summary>The two names on the algorithm — one drawer of history</summary>
Boris Weisfeiler and Andrei Leman published the refinement idea in 1968, in a
Soviet journal, as a heuristic step toward graph canonization — the "algebra
which appears therein" of their title is what we now call the coherent
configuration generated by a graph. Both later emigrated. Leman went into
software in Moscow and then abroad; Weisfeiler became a professor at Penn State
and a serious figure in algebraic groups. In January 1985, on a hiking trip in
Chile under the Pinochet regime, Boris Weisfeiler disappeared near a German
settler colony; his fate remains officially unresolved, and his sister spent
decades pressing the case. The algorithm the two left behind spent fifty years
as a niche tool of the isomorphism-testing community — polynomial-time, provably
incomplete, endlessly refinable into the k-WL hierarchy that Cai, Fürer and
Immerman mapped in 1992 — and then, in 2019, two independent papers (your
required reading among them) discovered that this exact algorithm is the ceiling
of the entire deep-learning-on-graphs enterprise. Fifty-one years from Soviet
algebra journal to the load-bearing theorem of a technology wave: file this in
the same drawer as PageRank's eigenvector and word2vec's PMI — the mathematics
was waiting.
</details>

## The object a GNN actually computes on

Why should a 1968 recoloring procedure bound a trained, continuous, attention-equipped neural network? Because both are functions of the same hidden object,
and that object is worth seeing raw.

Fix a node $v$ and unroll what $K$ rounds of message passing deliver to it: at
depth 1, its neighbors; at depth 2, their neighbors (including $v$ itself —
messages happily flow back); at depth $K$, every walk of length $K$ ending at
$v$. [Week 6](06-gcn.qmd) gave this object its name when it proved the
one-hop-per-layer claim; this week it carries the whole theory, so we restate
it:

::: {#def-w09-comp-tree .definition name="Computation tree"}
The **computation tree** of node $v$ to depth $K$ is the tree rooted at $v$
whose children are all neighbors of $v$, whose grandchildren are all neighbors
of *those* (the parent included), and so on for $K$ levels, with leaves
carrying the input features — equivalently, one branch per walk of length
$\le K$ ending at $v$. Reading guidance: everything a $K$-layer message-passing
model can ever know about $v$ is a function of this tree, and nothing else.
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w9-trees.html >}}

Every architecture from the past three weeks — GCN, SAGE, GAT, GATv2, GIN, with
any weights — computes $h_v^{(K)}$ by evaluating some function bottom-up on
exactly this tree: leaves get initial features, internal nodes combine their
children with the aggregator and update. The *graph* never enters except through
the tree.

Two details of the definition repay attention, because both are common sources
of wrong intuitions.

**Detail one: walks, not paths.** The children of a tree node are *all* neighbors —
including the one we just arrived from. The unrolling enumerates **walks**, not
paths: a walk may shuttle $v \to u \to v \to u$ forever, and the tree dutifully
records every shuttle. This is not sloppiness; it is fidelity. The GCN layer
really does send $v$'s round-1 state (which contains $u$'s influence) back to
$u$ in round 2, so echoes of yourself genuinely circulate, and the tree is
honest about it. It also means tree *size* explodes even on small graphs: a
degree-$d$ regular graph unrolls to $d^K$ leaves at depth $K$ — on the modest
hexagon, depth 10 already means $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ leaves feeding one node's
embedding, a number that will return with teeth in §7.

**Detail two: the tree forgets who the leaves are.** The tree forgets
exactly one thing about the graph, and it is the right thing to name precisely:
*which* leaves are the same node. In the triangle, the two depth-2 leaves under
different branches are literally one vertex; in the hexagon they are two. The
tree representation erases node identity across branches — and every blind spot
in this lecture, from cycle lengths to CSL, is downstream of precisely that
erasure. A model that could notice "these two leaves coincide" could count
cycles; message passing, by construction, cannot.

Which yields the week's central lemma:

::: {#prp-trees .proposition name="Trees determine embeddings"}
If two nodes $u, v$ — in the same
graph or in different graphs — have identical computation trees to depth $K$
(identical shapes and identical leaf features), then every $K$-layer
message-passing GNN assigns them identical embeddings, for every setting of the
weights. Moreover, two nodes have identical depth-$K$ trees exactly when 1-WL
gives them the same color after $K$ rounds.
:::

<details>
<summary>Proof sketch (induction both ways)</summary>
First claim, induction on $K$: at $K=0$ embeddings are the (equal) leaf features;
for the step, both nodes' children come in equal multisets of subtree-classes by
assumption, the inductive hypothesis makes the children's embeddings equal as
multisets, and aggregator plus update are functions of exactly (own embedding,
multiset of children embeddings) — the same inputs, the same output, regardless
of weights. Second claim, same induction: WL's round-$t$ color is by
construction a function of (own round-$(t\!-\!1)$ color, multiset of neighbors'
round-$(t\!-\!1)$ colors), which is precisely the recursive structure of the
depth-$t$ tree; conversely two nodes with the same round-$t$ color have, by
unrolling that recursion, isomorphic depth-$t$ trees. $\square$
</details>

Play with the middle preset in the widget above — it is the sharpest three
clicks in this lecture. $P_3$'s middle node and $P_4$'s second node have
*identical* trees at depth 1 (two children each) and *different* trees at depth
2 (one of $P_4$'s subtrees has an extra branch). One more layer flips the
verdict from "cannot be separated" to "can" — the cleanest possible
demonstration of what depth actually buys: not "more capacity" but *deeper
trees*, and deeper trees separate strictly more node pairs, until the trees stop
changing. And the molecules preset delivers the bad news of §2 in tree form: the
junction carbons of decalin and bicyclopentyl grow identical trees at every
depth, so no depth will ever help.

Chain the two propositions and the ceiling theorem falls out with almost
embarrassing ease. It was proved independently, fifty-one years after the
algorithm, by [Xu et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826) — your
required reading — and [Morris et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244):

::: {#thm-ceiling .theorem name="The 1-WL ceiling (Xu et al. 2019; Morris et al. 2019)"}
If 1-WL
assigns two graphs identical color histograms at every round, then every
message-passing GNN — any aggregator, any update, any attention, any depth, any
weights — assigns them identical multisets of node embeddings, hence identical
pooled representations. Message passing distinguishes *at most* what 1-WL
distinguishes.
:::

The proof is @prp-trees applied graph-wide: same histograms means the two
graphs' nodes pair up with identical trees, identical trees force identical
embeddings, and pooling a matching multiset gives a matching readout. Notice
what the theorem does *not* say: it does not say GNNs are weak, or that some
clever future aggregator escapes — the proof consumed *arbitrary* aggregators.
The only assumptions were "messages flow along edges" and "neighborhoods enter
as multisets." Everything in Weeks 6–8 lived inside those assumptions. To
escape the theorem you must break one of them, which is exactly what §6 does.

## GIN touches the ceiling — and why that isn't a leaderboard

The ceiling theorem is an upper bound. The natural next question: does anything
*reach* it? Week 7 built the answer without saying so.

::: {#thm-gin .theorem name="GIN matches 1-WL"}
A message-passing GNN whose layer is an *injective* function of the pair (own
state, neighbor multiset) distinguishes every pair of graphs that 1-WL
distinguishes — it reaches the ceiling. GIN realizes such a layer by

$$h_v^{(k+1)} = \mathrm{MLP}\!\left((1+\varepsilon)\, h_v^{(k)} + \sum_{u \in N(v)} h_u^{(k)}\right)$$ {#eq-w09-gin}

where — $h_v^{(k)}$ is node $v$'s embedding after $k$ layers ($h_v^{(0)}$ = the
input feature); $N(v)$ is $v$'s neighbor set; $\varepsilon \geq 0$ is a scalar
— fixed irrational or learned — that keeps "self" from colliding with the
neighbor sum; and $\mathrm{MLP}$ is a multi-layer perceptron (a fresh one per
layer), provided the input features come from a countable space embedded
injectively — one-hot colors suffice. Mean- and max-aggregating GNNs do not
reach the ceiling: they sit strictly below.
:::

<details>
<summary>Proof sketch, standing on Week 7's shoulders</summary>
Upper half: WL's recoloring is itself an injective function of (own color,
neighbor color multiset). If every GNN layer is injective on the same pair, then
by induction distinct WL colors at round $t$ yield distinct embeddings at layer
$t$ — the GNN simulates the refinement exactly, color for color. The work is
showing injectivity is realizable: over a countable feature space, map colors to
linearly independent embeddings and the *sum* of a bounded multiset determines
the multiset (your one-hot argument from the opener, formalized); the
$(1+\varepsilon)$ keeps "self" from colliding with "neighbors" (without it,
$h_v{=}a$ with neighbor sum $b$ ties $h_v{=}b$ with neighbor sum $a$); the MLP
supplies the arbitrary injective post-map, courtesy of universal approximation.
Lower half: mean of $\{t\}$ equals mean of $\{t,t\}$ and max of $\{t,t,g\}$
equals max of $\{t,g,g\}$ — the confusion cases you computed by hand in Lab 7
are not warm-ups; they are the counterexamples in the actual proof. $\square$
</details>

Read @eq-w09-gin once more, slowly, the way you would after this proof —
every symbol now has a job you can name.

- **The sum** is the injectivity workhorse: it alone preserves the multiset
  (Lab 7's hand computations were the lower half of this theorem, though we did
  not say so at the time).
- **The $(1+\varepsilon)$** is a tiny insurance policy against a specific
  collision: with $\varepsilon = 0$, a node in state $a$ whose neighbors sum to
  $b$ produces $a + b$ — indistinguishable from a node in state $b$ whose
  neighbors sum to $a$. Any irrational $\varepsilon$ (or a learned one, which
  is what `GINConv(train_eps=True)` does) breaks the tie by weighting "self"
  off the integer lattice. In practice, libraries default to $\varepsilon = 0$
  — the collision requires a coincidence real data rarely supplies, and the
  measured difference is noise; know the theory, then notice the field
  shrugging at it, and recognize the pattern from RotatE's constraints and
  GCN's self-loop trick: theoretical necessities often ship as optional flags.
- **The MLP** is not decoration but the universal-approximation half of the
  argument (*universal approximation*: a wide-enough MLP can match any
  continuous function to any accuracy — the classic result assumed from ML) —
  replace it with a single linear layer and injectivity of the *composite* can
  fail (a linear map can merge the very sums the aggregation kept apart), which
  is a second, subtler reading of why Week 6's one-matrix layers sit below this
  theorem.

And the theorem's fine print matters in the other direction too: the
guarantee is *existence* — suitable weights exist — not that gradient descent
finds them, a gap the next paragraph prices in dollars.

This is a beautiful result, and the discipline of Week 7 obliges us to read it
the way we read every beautiful claim: against a measured table. Here is the
uncomfortable row. In our own Cora ablation, GIN at depth 4 scored **44.2 ± 19.5**
— the most *expressive* architecture in the grid turned in the most unstable
result on the board, while the humble GCN, provably below the ceiling, sat at 81.

No contradiction: **expressiveness is a statement about what a network *can*
represent, not about what training *finds*, and not about what the task
*needs*.** Cora's task is smoothing labels over a homophilous graph — a job
below the ceiling — and GIN's sum, faithfully preserving degree information that
the task treats as noise, hands the optimizer a harder landscape for zero usable
capacity. Expressiveness matters exactly when the task's signal lives in what
the weaker model cannot see (molecular rings, §5's counterexamples) — and there
it is not a nicety but the difference between possible and impossible. Everywhere
else, it is free variance. "More expressive" is an axis, not an endorsement; you
now own both the theorem and the error bar, and the pairing is the point.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** 1-WL cannot distinguish two triangles from a hexagon
— graphs with *different numbers of triangles* (2 versus 0). What does that
imply about any message-passing GNN asked to compute the clustering coefficient
from [Week 2](02-classical-graph-ml.qmd)?

::: {.predict-answer}
It cannot, not even approximately-in-the-worst-case: clustering coefficient is a
function of triangle counts, the blind pair differs in triangle count while
receiving identical embeddings, so any function the GNN computes returns the
same value for both — the true answers differ, hence the error is bounded away
from zero *no matter the training data*. A feature you computed with three lines
of NetworkX in Week 2 is provably out of reach of every architecture in Weeks
6–8. Hold that thought for §6, where the cheapest fix is literally "give the
network Week 2's features."
:::
:::

## An atlas of the invisible

What, concretely, lives above the ceiling? A tour of the blind spots, each one a
graph pair with identical WL histograms, each hand-checkable. One line of
notation for the tour: $C_n$ is the cycle on $n$ nodes, $P_n$ the path on $n$
nodes, and $K_n$ the complete graph — so $K_2$ is a single edge.

**Cycle lengths.** The founding example: $C_3 \cup C_3$ versus $C_6$, and more
generally $C_n \cup C_m$ versus $C_{n+m}$ — every 2-regular graph of a given
size looks identical to WL. Message passing cannot measure the length of the
loop it is standing on. Consequence: triangle counts, clustering coefficients,
odd-cycle detection are all invisible on regular inputs — and note what the
last one implies: *bipartiteness*, arguably the single most consequential
yes/no property a graph has (it decided when random-walk returns vanish in
Week 2 and which spectra symmetrize in Week 6), is undecidable from inside the
message-passing box.

**Anything on regular graphs.** On a $d$-regular graph with uniform features,
round 1 recolors every node identically — everyone reports "degree $d$, all
neighbors my color" — and induction keeps it that way forever: WL's partition
never leaves "everyone," no matter how many rounds you grant it. *Any two* $d$-regular graphs
on $n$ nodes — connected or not, planar or not, bipartite or not — receive
identical histograms. Regularity is WL's kryptonite, which motivates the sharpest
family of test cases the field has:

**CSL graphs.** The community's stress-test family makes the regularity failure
maximally concrete, and it earns its place in benchmarks precisely because it
is so easy to build and so hard to see. Take 11 nodes in a ring, connect each
to its neighbors at distance 1 and at distance $s$ — the *circulant skip-link*
graph $\mathrm{CSL}(11, s)$. Both $\mathrm{CSL}(11,2)$ and $\mathrm{CSL}(11,3)$ are
4-regular, so WL sees "everyone, forever" on both; they are provably
non-isomorphic (Lab 9 has you verify both facts in four lines). Yet the
difference is not subtle — you can *count* it. In $\mathrm{CSL}(11,2)$, skips of
2 close triangles ($1+1=2$), three of them through every node; in
$\mathrm{CSL}(11,3)$, no combination of steps from $\{\pm1, \pm3\}$ closes in
three moves, so there are none. A 3-step random walk returns home with
probability $6/64 \approx 0.094$ in the first graph and $0$ in the second. The
structure screams; the test is deaf.

**Distances and bottlenecks.** WL is resolutely local: two graphs can differ in
diameter, in connectivity (the blind pair already does — one is disconnected!),
in whether removing an edge splits them, while WL shrugs. Global shape is not
in the tree.

**Substructure counting, graded precisely.** The counting story has been mapped
theorem by theorem, and the map is more interesting than a blanket "GNNs can't
count." Message passing *can* count structures that embed into trees: your own
degree, stars around you, edges — anything whose shape survives unrolling. It
provably *cannot* count structures that require noticing a walk closed —
triangles, cycles of any fixed length, cliques — because closure is exactly the
leaf-identity information the tree erased. The boundary is the tree-shape of
the pattern, not its size: a 10-node star is countable, a 3-node triangle is
not. This graded picture is why the practical fix in §6 is so surgical — you do
not need a new architecture class to see triangles; you need three lines of
Week 2 NetworkX appended to the features, and the theorem's objection is
answered at the exact point it was raised.

The atlas explains a benchmark pattern you will meet in the wild. The standard
molecular benchmark ZINC asks models to predict a quantity (constrained
solubility) that depends explicitly on ring counts — a property just shown to
be invisible — and the leaderboard's history reads like this lecture's outline:
plain message passing plateaus, models with cycle-aware features or positional
encodings jump, and the current top entries all carry some structural
augmentation from §6. Meanwhile on citation-style homophily tasks the ceiling
never binds, and "more expressive" buys only §4's variance. Diagnosing *which
regime your task is in* is worth more than any architecture choice, and it is
the skill §8 drills.

## Drilling through

The ceiling theorem's assumptions were two: messages flow along edges, and nodes
begin anonymous — nothing distinguishes a node beyond its features. Every escape
route breaks one of the two. The field has settled into four families, and they
form a ladder:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w9-ladder.html >}}

**Route 1: tell the nodes who they are (identity features).** Give every node a
unique ID, or a random vector, and the anonymity assumption shatters: no two
computation trees ever match, WL separates everything, and GNNs with random
features become provably universal approximators on graphs
([Abboud et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01179)).
Sounds like a free lunch; the widget below is the bill. Separating *everything*
includes separating two relabeled copies of the *same* graph — the network can
now memorize "node 7 is special" in training and mean nothing by it at test
time. Permutation invariance, the property [Week 6](06-gcn.qmd) spent a
proposition earning, was purchased by exactly the anonymity we just sold.

**Route 2: tell the nodes what they are (structural features).** Compute
permutation-respecting quantities and append them to the features: per-node
triangle counts (three lines of Week 2), $k$-step random-walk return
probabilities (Week 2's PageRank machinery pointed at itself), Laplacian
eigenvector coordinates (Week 6's frequencies, reborn as *positional
encodings*). Structural features are functions of the graph, so isomorphic
copies agree — the honesty of anonymity, with strictly more sight. The
random-walk member of that menu earns a listing, both because Lab 9 has you
build it (`rw_return_probs`) and because, under the name RWPE
([Dwivedi et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07875)), it has become a
standard ingredient of graph transformers:

::: {#alg-w09-rwpe .algorithm name="Random-Walk Return Features (RWPE)"}
Computes, for every node, the probability that a $k$-step random walk starting
there returns home — a structural signature no relabeling can disturb.

**Input:** graph $G$ with adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and degree matrix
$\mathbf{D}$; number of steps $k_{\max}$. **Output:** feature vector
$r(v) \in \mathbb{R}^{k_{\max}}$ per node.

1. $\mathbf{M} \leftarrow \mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{A}$ (the random-walk operator, Week 2)
2. $\mathbf{P} \leftarrow \mathbf{I}$
3. **for** $k = 1 \ldots k_{\max}$ **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\mathbf{P} \leftarrow \mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}$
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$r_k(v) \leftarrow \mathbf{P}[v, v]$ for every $v$
6. **end for**
7. **return** $r(v) = \bigl(r_1(v), \ldots, r_{k_{\max}}(v)\bigr)$, appended to $\mathbf{x}_v$
:::

Line 5 reads the diagonal of a matrix power — the probability that a $k$-step
walk from $v$ ends back at $v$ — so the whole computation is $k_{\max}$ sparse
matrix multiplies, done once as preprocessing. Because every quantity is a
function of the graph alone, two isomorphic copies get identical features:
the honesty test passes by construction. The RW
returns you can hand-verify on CSL ($0.094$ vs $0$ at three steps) are, almost
verbatim, the RWPE inputs of current graph-transformer stacks
([Rampášek et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12454)).

The
eigenvector option must handle one wrinkle you already know from Week 6: an
eigenvector is only defined up to sign (and, in degenerate eigenspaces, up to
rotation), so the "position" handed to node $v$ depends on choices the graph
never made. If you train with one sign and test with the flip, the encoding
betrays you exactly the way random IDs do — so practitioners either randomize
signs during training (teaching the network the invariance by augmentation),
take absolute values (cheap, lossy), or use architectures that consume
eigenvectors invariantly. It is Week 6's "coordinates across runs" leak
detector, resurfacing one abstraction level higher, and it is why the
random-walk encodings — which have no sign to flip — have quietly become the
default choice in the graph-transformer literature: every large "graphs as
sequences plus positional encodings" model you will meet is spending this
paragraph's trade-offs, made industrial.

The deeper pattern deserves a
sentence of its own: *positional encodings are the graph reasserting itself
after the tree erased it.* WL forgot which leaves coincide; a positional
encoding writes a summary of the erased identity back into the features, sized
to your budget — one scalar (triangle count), a $k$-vector (RW returns), or a
full spectral address (Laplacian coordinates).

Put both routes on trial simultaneously — the widget scores every augmentation
on the two questions that matter, *does it separate different graphs* and *does
it spare the same graph*:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w9-power.html >}}

**Route 3: color richer objects (higher-order WL).** Instead of refining node
colors, refine colors of node *pairs* (or $k$-tuples): 2-tuples know whether
their endpoints are adjacent, and refinement over tuples sees structure
invisible to nodes. This is the $k$-WL hierarchy, and it is strict: for every
$k$ there are graphs $k$-WL confuses and $(k{+}1)$-WL separates (the Cai–Fürer–
Immerman construction, 1992 — pre-dating the deep-learning application by
twenty-seven years). 3-WL separates the CSL family natively, no features
needed. The price is printed on the tin: $n^2$ or $n^3$ objects to color means
$O(n^2)$–$O(n^3)$ memory and worse time — on a 100,000-node graph, node-pairs
alone number $10^{10}$. Higher-order GNNs (your optional reading) implement
exactly this trade and are the reason "provably more powerful than 1-WL" papers
tend to report results on small molecules, not on ogbn-arxiv.

A fourth family sits *between* the ladder's rungs — the figure draws it as a
half-rung: **subgraph GNNs**
([Bevilacqua et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.02910)), the field's
current favorite compromise.
Instead of enriching features or coloring tuples, run an ordinary
message-passing GNN on a *bag of perturbed copies* of the input — delete one
node per copy, or mark one node per copy — and aggregate the bag. Two
WL-identical graphs rarely stay identical after you delete a node from each
(delete a triangle vertex from $C_3 \cup C_3$ and a component vanishes; delete
any vertex of $C_6$ and you get a path — instantly distinguishable), so the bag
sees strictly more than any single run, at a cost of $n$ GNN evaluations rather
than $n^2$ memory: between the ladder's rungs both in power and in price.
The construction should feel familiar — it is the ablation instinct of Week 7
promoted into an architecture: *perturb, re-measure, and let the differences
speak*.

**Route 4: change the graph (rewiring / global links).** If messages only flow
along edges, add edges: a virtual "master node" connected to everything, a
fully-adjacent final layer, or surgical shortcuts. This route is really aimed at
the week's *second* wall, so it gets its own section —

## The second wall: oversquashing

Expressiveness asked what the architecture can represent. There is a humbler
failure mode that arrives first in practice: the information is representable,
reachable, *and does not fit through the pipe*.

Count what a receptive field costs. With branching factor $b$, the depth-$K$
computation tree holds on the order of $b^K$ leaves — at $b=3$, $K=8$, over six
thousand sources — and all of it must flow into one fixed-width vector at the
root. Worse, the flow is not evenly bottlenecked: if the graph has a narrow cut,
everything crossing it squeezes through a handful of edges regardless of width.
The phenomenon was named and isolated by
[Alon & Yahav, 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05205), your required reading:

::: {#def-w09-oversquash .definition name="Oversquashing"}
**Oversquashing** is the loss of long-range signal that occurs when a receptive
field of exponentially many sources must flow through fixed-width node vectors
— exponentially many messages, polynomially many wires — worst at *bottleneck*
edges, the narrow cuts everything must cross. Reading guidance: the distant
information is reachable and representable; it is crushed *in transit*, the
gradient across the bottleneck attenuating until distant signal is effectively
unlearnable.
:::

You do not have to take "attenuates" on faith; it is a number, and we computed
it. Define the $K$-layer **sensitivity** of target $v$ to source $u$ as

$$S^{(K)}_{uv} = \left(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^K\right)_{uv}$$ {#eq-w09-sens}

where — $\hat{\mathbf{A}} = \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I})\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}$
is Week 6's normalized propagation operator (adjacency plus self-loops,
degree-discounted), $K$ is the number of layers, and the entry $(u, v)$ of its
$K$-th power totals every length-$\le K$ walk between the two nodes, each
discounted by the degrees along the way. @eq-w09-sens is the exact influence in
a linear propagation model, kin to the Jacobian bounds in the rewiring
literature, and Lab 9's exercise 5 builds it verbatim. Now point it at two
5-cliques joined by a two-node path:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w9-squash.html >}}

Within the source's own clique, influence sits near $0.18$. Across the bridge —
five hops, every route through the same two path nodes — it is $6 \times
10^{-4}$: a **290×** crush. And the diagnosis dictates the cure with unusual
directness: add *one* edge across, changing nothing about depth or width, and
the far side's influence jumps 25-fold. Run it live, and mind the K-stepper's
lesson at the low end — at $K \le 4$ the far clique's influence is exactly
zero, which is *unreachability* (a receptive-field problem, solved by depth),
not oversquashing (a bottleneck problem, that depth alone cannot solve):

{{< include ../assets/d3/w9-squash.html >}}

The paper that named the phenomenon also supplied the cleanest instrument for
isolating it, and the design is worth studying as method, not just result.
Alon & Yahav built **Tree-NeighborsMatch**: a synthetic task on complete binary
trees where the answer at the root depends on matching information stored at
the leaves, depth $r$ away — nothing to memorize, nothing structural to
confuse, just information that must travel from $2^r$ leaves to one root
through the tree's narrowing waist. Every standard architecture — GCN, SAGE,
GAT, GIN — fails *abruptly* at a characteristic depth (most around $r = 4$;
accuracy falls off a cliff rather than degrading), and the failure survives
unlimited training data and generous width. Because the task is synthetic, no
rival explanation survives: the receptive field is sufficient (the tree *is*
reachable), expressiveness is sufficient (the function is tree-computable —
even 1-WL sees it), so what remains is the pipe.

Then the punchline fix: make
the **last layer fully adjacent** — every node exchanges one round of messages
with every node — and performance jumps, on the synthetic task and on real
chemistry benchmarks, for one layer's cost. That experimental shape — a
synthetic that isolates one mechanism, an ablation that names the cure — is
Week 7's discipline producing a theorem-grade insight without a theorem, and it
is the reason this paper is required reading rather than the heavier formal
follow-ups.

(Those exist: the curvature line of work in your optional reading
formalizes the bottleneck via Jacobian sensitivity bounds — our
$(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ is the linear special case — and locates squashing at
negatively curved edges, bridges being the canonical example. The barbell you
just played with is their Figure 1, in miniature.)

Keep the week's two walls apart — they get conflated constantly, they co-occur
in deep models, and their fixes point in *opposite directions*:

| | oversmoothing | oversquashing |
|---|---|---|
| **what happens** | representations converge toward one dominant direction | distant signal is crushed through narrow cuts |
| **cause** | repeated averaging: powers of $\hat A$ kill non-dominant components at rate $\|\lambda_2\|^K$ ($\lambda_2$: $\hat A$'s second-largest eigenvalue by magnitude, Week 6) | exponential receptive field vs fixed-width vectors and bottleneck edges |
| **you measured it** | HW2: karate contraction rate $=$ $\|\lambda_2\|$ to two decimals | this page: $0.18$ vs $6\times10^{-4}$ across the barbell bridge |
| **worsens when** | depth grows on a *well-connected* graph | the task needs *long-range* signal on a *narrow-cut* graph |
| **repair** | fewer layers, residuals, restart/normalization ([Week 7's repair shop](07-gnn-design.qmd)) | rewiring, master node, fully-adjacent last layer, global attention |
| **danger of the wrong fix** | rewiring a smoothing model densifies the graph and smooths *faster* | adding residual depth to a squashing model deepens the tree without widening the cut |

The last row is why the distinction earns a table: the cures are antagonists.
Rewiring accelerates smoothing; depth aggravates squashing. Diagnose first —
which is precisely the skill this week's method section turns into a checklist.

Where does squashing actually bite, outside synthetic trees and barbells? Wherever
the task couples *distant* nodes across *narrow* structure. Molecules whose
property depends on two functional groups at opposite ends of a chain — the
chemistry benchmarks where Alon & Yahav's one-layer fix produced its real-world
gains. Program graphs, where a variable's definition and its (mis)use sit many
syntactic hops apart. Mesh and road networks, all corridors and few shortcuts.

The pattern was strong enough that the field built a dedicated benchmark suite
([Dwivedi et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08164))
— long-range graph tasks where local models flatline by construction — and it
is on exactly those leaderboards that global-attention models earn their extra
cost. Contrast Cora one final time: citation neighborhoods are shallow, the
label signal is local, and none of this section's machinery would move the
number — which you can now say *before* running the experiment, and that is the
entire point of owning the distinction.

## The method: diagnosing a failing GNN

Weeks 6–8 gave you architectures; this week gives you the theory of their
limits; here is the procedure that connects the two when a model underperforms
and you must decide *why* before deciding what to change. Five checks, in order
of cost — the table is the checklist, the paragraphs after it are the manual:

| # | check | the cheap experiment | what it decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | fit before ceiling | overfit a small training subset | broken training/bugs vs a real limit |
| 2 | the task's altitude | linear probe on the suspect structural feature | whether the ceiling is even binding |
| 3 | cheapest fix first | append triangle counts / RW returns, retrain | feature fix vs architecture escalation |
| 4 | separate the two walls | $(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ probe vs cosine-by-layer plot | squashing vs smoothing |
| 5 | trees, not vibes | run WL on a suspicious input pair | whether *any* message-passing change can help |

**Check the fit before the ceiling.** Can the model overfit a small training
subset to ~100%? If not, your problem is optimization or bugs, not
expressiveness — no theorem in this lecture is about you. (This one-minute test
would have caught depth-4 GAT's crash in Week 7 before any theory was
consulted.)

**Check the task's altitude.** Does the label plausibly depend on structure WL
cannot see — ring sizes, motif counts, global distances? Estimate directly:
compute the suspect structural feature (Week 2 skills), measure its correlation
with the label, or better, feed it to a *linear* probe. Signal in the probe +
plateaued GNN = the ceiling is binding.

**Run the cheapest fix first.** Append triangle counts / RW returns to the
features and retrain. If the plateau breaks, you have both the diagnosis and,
quite possibly, the shipped solution — structural features cost preprocessing,
not architecture. Only escalate to higher-order models when feature engineering
demonstrably saturates *and* the gap justifies $O(n^2)$ or worse.

**Separate the two walls.** Long-range task on a bottlenecked graph
(molecules with far-apart functional groups, meshes, road networks)? Probe with
the sensitivity matrix: tiny $(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ for task-relevant pairs at
reachable depth is oversquashing — rewire or globalize. Representations
collapsing across *all* nodes as depth grows (check pairwise cosine similarity
by layer, as in Lab 9) is oversmoothing — shorten, skip, or restart, per the
table above.

**Audit with trees, not vibes.** If two inputs your task must separate get
suspiciously similar outputs, run WL on the pair (milliseconds) — matching
histograms mean *no* message-passing change will ever separate them, and the
conversation moves to features or higher order. A negative WL check has saved
teams months of architecture search; it is the cheapest theorem application in
this course.

To see the checklist earn its keep, run our own Week-7 embarrassment through
it. GIN·4 at 44.2 ± 19.5 on Cora: check one — can it overfit a training
subset? Yes, quickly, so the architecture is not broken and no ceiling is
implicated. Check two — does Cora's label depend on WL-invisible structure? A
triangle-count probe adds nothing over the word features, so the task sits well
below the ceiling and expressiveness arguments are beside the point. Check
four — collapsing representations with depth, per the cosine-by-layer plot?
Yes, plus a 19.5-point standard deviation screaming optimization instability.
Verdict in under ten minutes: an oversmoothing-plus-training problem wearing an
expressive architecture, cure on the Week-7 shelf (residuals rescued GAT·4 from
26 to 80; the same edit lifts GIN), and no theorem from this lecture required —
only the discipline of asking the questions in order. The habit underneath all
five: **failure modes are hypotheses, and each has a cheap experiment.** That
was Week 7's ablation discipline pointed at theory instead of hyperparameters,
and it is the version of this lecture you will still be using when GIN is a
historical footnote.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reading “same embeddings” as “same graphs”" icon="false"}
WL and GNNs convict, never
acquit (@prp-sound). A GNN mapping two graphs together is silence, not
similarity — on the sample exam, roughly a third of last year's cohort got the
direction wrong on the equivalent question. *(The 2025 cohort took a different
course — but the error statistic travels; it is the single most common
theory mistake in this field's papers, too.)*
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Expressiveness rankings read as performance rankings" icon="false"}
GIN ≥ GCN on
the ladder; GIN scored 44 to GCN's 81 on our measured Cora grid. The ladder
orders what is *representable*; tasks, optimizers, and noise decide what is
*learned*. Cite both numbers when someone proposes an architecture change "for
expressiveness."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · Random features as a free upgrade" icon="false"}
They break the ceiling *and* the
invariance that made GNNs generalize across relabelings. If you must use them
(some tasks warrant it), test on permuted copies of training graphs — the
widget's pair-B check, industrialized.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Confusing unreachable with squashed" icon="false"}
If the target is outside the
receptive field, depth fixes it; if it is inside but crushed through a cut,
depth *worsens* it. One is a radius problem, the other a topology problem —
the K-stepper on the barbell widget is the two-minute drill.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · Fixing the wrong wall" icon="false"}
Residuals for a squashing model, rewiring for a
smoothing one — both make things worse, per the table. No repair before
diagnosis.
:::

## In this week's lab

[Lab 9](../labs/lab09.qmd) makes every claim of this lecture executable: you
implement WL refinement from scratch and drive it over the blind pairs; verify
with an untrained GIN that identical WL colors force identical embeddings (and
that a WL-splittable pair splits); build the CSL graphs and watch degree,
uniform, and random features fail the two-question trial while RW returns pass
it; and measure the barbell's sensitivity crush plus its one-edge rescue,
reproducing this page's 290× and 25× to the decimal. Everything is deterministic
— no seeds to blame, exactly like the theory deserves.

## Required reading

- **[Xu, Hu, Leskovec, Jegelka — How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826)** (ICLR
  2019). The ceiling and the touch: Theorem 3, Corollary 6, and Figure 2's
  one-picture summary of sum vs mean vs max. Reproduce Figure 3's pairs by hand
  — that is the self-test that matters.
- **[Alon & Yahav — On the Bottleneck of Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.05205)** (ICLR 2021).
  Oversquashing named, isolated (Tree-NeighborsMatch), and cheaply fixed;
  read it as a masterclass in diagnostic experiment design.

Optional: [Morris et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.02244) (AAAI 2019) for
the k-WL staircase; [Li, Han & Wu](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07606) (AAAI
2018) for oversmoothing's original diagnosis;
[Topping et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.14522) (ICLR 2022) for
oversquashing through the lens of curvature — the mathematical deep end of this
week's pool.

## Check your understanding

The exam bank draws from exactly this style of question.

**Q1.** Run WL on $C_4$ versus $2 \times K_2$ (four nodes each). Which round
splits them, and what does the split prove?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Round 1: $C_4$'s nodes all have degree 2, $2K_2$'s all have degree 1 — the
histograms differ immediately ($\{4\}$ under color "saw two" versus $\{4\}$
under color "saw one"; different colors, different histograms). The split
*proves* non-isomorphism (soundness). Note the trap the question sets: both
histograms are "all four nodes one class" — but the classes are different
colors, and the shared HASH table is what makes them comparable.
</details>

**Q2.** Your colleague's GNN gives identical embeddings to two molecules with
different boiling points and concludes "the molecules are structurally
identical." Correct the conclusion in one sentence.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Identical embeddings are silence, not similarity: message passing is bounded by
1-WL, which can fail to separate non-isomorphic graphs (decalin vs
bicyclopentyl), so the only valid conclusions flow from *different* embeddings —
these two molecules may simply sit above the model's ceiling.
</details>

**Q3.** Every node of $\mathrm{CSL}(11,2)$ and $\mathrm{CSL}(11,3)$ has degree
4. Compute the 3-step return probability of a random walk in each, and explain
what a GNN with RW-return features can now do that it provably could not before.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$\mathrm{CSL}(11,2)$: skips $\{\pm1,\pm2\}$ close three triangles through each
node, each contributing two closed 3-walks: $6/4^3 = 0.094$. In
$\mathrm{CSL}(11,3)$ no elements of $\{\pm1,\pm3\}$ sum to zero in three steps:
probability $0$. With those numbers as features, round-0 colors already differ
between the graphs, so refinement — and hence any GNN reading the features —
separates a pair that anonymous message passing provably cannot (both graphs
are 4-regular, so 1-WL never splits either).
</details>

**Q4.** State the two assumptions the ceiling theorem consumes, and name the
escape route that breaks each.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Assumption 1: nodes start anonymous (features carry no identity) — broken by
identity/random features (dangerously) or structural/positional features
(honestly). Assumption 2: information flows only along edges, neighborhoods
entering as multisets — broken by rewiring, master nodes, global attention, or
by coloring higher-order tuples instead of nodes (k-WL / higher-order GNNs).
</details>

**Q5.** A 12-layer model on a diameter-4 graph shows all node representations
converging with depth. Which wall is this, what measurement confirms it, and
which two fixes from this week apply?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Oversmoothing: depth far beyond diameter adds no new information sources and
keeps applying the low-pass operator; confirm by measuring pairwise cosine
similarity per layer (Lab 9) or the contraction rate against $|\lambda_2|$
(HW2). Fixes: cut depth toward the diameter, add residual/restart connections
(Week 7). Rewiring — the *other* wall's fix — would densify the graph and
smooth faster.
</details>

**Q6.** Why does appending a node's triangle count to its features preserve
permutation invariance, while appending its row index does not?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Triangle count is a function of the graph's structure at that node: any
isomorphism maps a node to a node with the same count, so relabeled copies get
identical feature-augmented representations. A row index is a function of the
*labeling*: relabeling changes it, two copies of the same graph stop matching,
and the invariance Week 6 proved for message passing is silently destroyed.
</details>

**Q7.** GIN is provably more expressive than GCN, yet scored 37 points lower at
depth 4 in our Cora grid. Reconcile in two sentences.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Expressiveness bounds what is representable; Cora's homophilous label-smoothing
task needs nothing above GCN's reach, so GIN's extra capacity buys no signal.
Meanwhile sum aggregation preserves degree/count information the task treats as
noise, yielding a harder optimization landscape — hence 44.2 ± 19.5 versus 81:
an axis, not an endorsement, measured.
</details>

**Q8.** Design the one-minute experiment that decides whether a plateaued model
on long-range molecular data is bottlenecked (squashing) rather than
under-expressive.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Alon & Yahav's trick: make the *final* layer fully adjacent (every node talks to
every node once) and retrain. That single change widens the cut without touching
expressiveness class or depth; if performance jumps, the model was squashed, not
blind — and you learned it for the cost of one run. (A complementary probe:
compute $(\hat A^K)_{uv}$ for task-critical distant pairs and compare against
within-neighborhood values, as on the barbell.)
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **WL color refinement, two-graph form** (@eq-w09-wl, @alg-w09-wl-compare) — recolor every node by (own color, neighbor-color multiset) under ONE table shared across both graphs; compare histograms per round.
- **WL-distinguishable / WL abstains** (@def-w09-wl-dist) — differing histograms convict; matching histograms are silence, never sameness (@prp-sound).
- **Computation tree** (@def-w09-comp-tree) — the depth-$K$ unrolling of a node's neighborhood: walks, not paths; leaf identity erased.
- **Trees determine embeddings** (@prp-trees) — identical trees force identical embeddings for every weight setting; tree classes = WL colors.
- **The 1-WL ceiling** (@thm-ceiling) — message passing distinguishes at most what 1-WL distinguishes, for any aggregator, attention, or depth.
- **GIN / injective aggregation** (@thm-gin, @eq-w09-gin) — sum-then-MLP with the $(1+\varepsilon)$ self-term reaches the ceiling; mean and max sit below.
- **CSL graphs** — circulant skip-link rings: 4-regular, WL-blind, provably non-isomorphic — the field's stress-test family.
- **Structural / positional features** (@alg-w09-rwpe) — permutation-respecting quantities (triangle counts, RW returns, Laplacian coordinates) appended to features: separation without the random-ID lie.
- **k-WL hierarchy and subgraph GNNs** — color $k$-tuples ($O(n^k)$ cost) or aggregate a bag of perturbed copies ($n$ GNN runs): the ladder's upper rungs and its half-rung.
- **Sensitivity** (@eq-w09-sens) — $(\hat{A}^K)_{uv}$, the exact linear influence of $u$ on $v$; the number that separates unreachable (exactly 0) from squashed (tiny).
- **Oversquashing** (@def-w09-oversquash) — exponentially many messages through polynomially many wires; antagonist of oversmoothing, with opposite cures.
:::

## Where this leaves us

Three weeks of building ended, this week, in a map of the building's limits: the
object message passing computes on (a tree), the fifty-year-old algorithm that
bounds it (1-WL), the architecture that meets the bound (GIN), the atlas of what
lives above it (cycles, regular families, global shape), the honest ways up
(structure you compute, tuples you color), and the second wall that arrives
before the first (a bridge, crushing 290× of signal into two path nodes). You
measured everything measurable: the return probabilities, the sensitivities, the
rescue factor. And you left with a diagnostic procedure, because in this course
theory earns its seat by telling you *what experiment to run next* — a standard
this lecture's two required papers themselves set, each pairing its theorem
with the cheap experiment that makes the theorem undeniable.

Close the loop — one minute, no notes: one round of @alg-w09-wl-compare on the
blind pair and the verdict rule; the tail node's $k{=}3$ return and what that
entry detects; the 290× bridge number and the sensitivity that measures it; the
three routes above 1-WL; and GIN's design equation. Each is an exam question in
embryo.

Notice, finally, an assumption that every graph in this lecture shared — one so
quiet you may not have registered it as an assumption at all. Every edge meant
the *same thing*. The karate club's edges were all friendship; Cora's were all
citation; the barbell's were all wire. But the knowledge graphs of Weeks 4–5
laughed at that premise — *treats*, *targets*, *located_in* — and we handled it
then by giving every relation its own geometry and abandoning message passing
entirely. Next week the two threads finally merge: message passing over graphs
with **many kinds of nodes and many kinds of edges** — academic graphs where
authors write papers that appear at venues, and FB15k-237 itself with a
message-passing encoder (R-GCN) replacing the lookup table. The filing cabinet
of Week 4 meets the template of Week 7, and the first question — you can
already guess it — will be *what one weight matrix per relation costs when there
are 237 of them*.
